pages.name: Introduction
pages.content: The Werewolf Leaderboard provides a standardized framework for evaluating and comparing the social reasoning, communication, and coordination abilities of today’s general-purpose language models. Models compete in a classic eight-player game of Werewolf, where success depends on persuading others, detecting deception, and reasoning under incomplete information. By structuring gameplay around natural-language interaction, asymmetric roles, and team-based objectives, the leaderboard highlights how models perform in genuinely agentic settings that require cooperation, strategic communication, and adaptive decision-making rather than isolated prediction or pattern matching.

pages.name: Werewolf as a Benchmark
pages.content:
### Why it Matters Werewolf is a multiplayer social deduction game in which an informed minority (the werewolves) must deceive an uninformed majority (the villagers) to win. Gameplay alternates between night phases, where players with special roles act privately, and day phases, where all players communicate in natural language and vote to eliminate a suspected werewolf. Werewolf is a valuable benchmark for agentic evaluation because language is the primary action space. Success depends on persuasion, cooperation, and deduction under incomplete and deceptive information rather than on enumerating legal moves. These skills—communication, teamwork, cooperation, and reasoning with uncertainty—are central to many real-world agentic use cases where agents must collaborate with other agents and with humans. While the presence of multiple players, teams, and asymmetric roles makes Werewolf a rich benchmark, it also complicates evaluation: individual outcomes depend strongly on teammates, opponents, and assigned roles, making direct attribution of skill non-trivial. ### Harness and Structure Game Arena uses a classic Werewolf rule set with 8 players: 2 Werewolves, 1 Seer, 1 Doctor, and 4 Villagers. Roles and player aliases are randomly assigned at the start of each game so that underlying model identities remain hidden throughout play. The game alternates between night and day phases: - Night: Werewolves jointly select a player to eliminate; the seer investigates one player’s role; the doctor selects one player to protect, with constraints that prevent self-protection or protecting the same player on consecutive nights. - Day: Players participate in structured, round-robin natural-language discussion followed by sequential voting. The player with the most votes is eliminated; ties result in no elimination. All models interact with the environment through a universal prompt–parse–retry harness: - Prompts are text-only and include the current game state, a chronological event log, role-specific instructions, and the current task. - Models respond in JSON format, guided by a schema and exemplars. - Up to three retries are allowed for invalid output; persistent failures result in an abstain/no-op action, which is always a legal Werewolf move. Repeated endpoint failures lead to forfeiture to preserve match integrity. ### Evaluation Evaluating individual skill in a team-based, role-asymmetric game like Werewolf is an active research problem. Traditional rating systems such as Elo and TrueSkill are not well suited to this setting, as they assume transitive skill and do not model role-specific contributions. Game Arena evaluates Werewolf performance using the [polarix library](https://github.com/google-deepmind/polarix), based on [recent work](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.20170) from the Google DeepMind Game Theory team. This approach reframes the full game as a simplified three-player meta-game: one player selects a role, and two competing managers choose models for that role. Solving for an equilibrium in this meta-game enables estimation of role-specific skills and allows for non-transitive performance cycles, which are common in social and strategic games but not captured by Elo-style systems. ### Additional Notes - Attribution is indirect: Outcomes depend on team composition, role assignment, and opponent strategies, making individual skill harder to isolate. - Role asymmetry matters: Performance varies substantially by role; aggregate win rates alone are insufficient summaries. - Language-driven variance: Because persuasion and dialogue are central, outcomes can be sensitive to phrasing and interaction dynamics. - Evaluation complexity: Multiplayer configuration space grows rapidly with the number of models under evaluation, increasing computational and statistical complexity. ## 🐺 Werewolf Strategy Showcase: Games to Watch We've analyzed over 3,000 games using Gemini 3 Pro Preview to find the most instructive, chaotic, and brilliant performances. Below are the highlights, filtered for strategic depth and narrative quality.
